name: CLAT UG
fullName: Common Law Admission Test – Undergraduate (5-year integrated LL.B.)
eligibility: 10+2 with 45% (40% for SC/ST); candidates appearing in Class 12 in March/April 2027 may apply; no upper age limit

notification.summary: The Consortium of NLUs notified CLAT 2027 on 22 Jul 2026. Online applications opened on 3 Aug 2026 and are open until 31 Oct 2026; the pen-and-paper exam is on Sunday 6 Dec 2026 (2–4 pm). The Consortium has said the syllabus and pattern are unchanged. Checked via web search on 2026-10-10 (news/coaching reports citing consortiumofnlus.ac.in).

pattern.notes: Officially the section ranges are English 22–26, Current Affairs 28–32, Legal 28–32, Logical 22–26 and Quantitative 10–14 questions; the mock uses mid-range values. Every section is passage/caselet based (passages of roughly 300–450 words, each followed by 4–6 questions); in this mock each question carries its own short passage. No sectional time limit.

trendAnalysis.summary: Since CLAT 2024 the paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes (down from 150), all passage-based. Legal Reasoning and Current Affairs carry the most weight (≈25% each); legal passages increasingly draw on recent statutes and judgments (BNS/BNSS, data protection, constitutional cases), but answers still follow strictly from the principle stated. Current Affairs passages cover the 12–15 months before the exam, with questions frequently testing related static facts (constitutional articles, institutions, treaties). English passages are long but moderate; Logical Reasoning focuses on argument analysis rather than puzzles; Quant is class-10 arithmetic in caselet form. CLAT 2026 (Dec 2025) was rated moderate overall, with lengthy legal passages and a time-consuming quant section.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the Consortium of NLUs' published question papers and answer keys for CLAT 2024, CLAT 2025 and CLAT 2026 (held 3 Dec 2023, 1 Dec 2024 and 7 Dec 2025) as summarised in post-exam analyses (IMS, Hitbullseye, LegalEdge, CLAT NLTI) found via web search; the full papers could not be fetched in this session, so section-wise question types were consolidated from those analyses and the writer's own knowledge. Notable 2026 shift: Logical Reasoning carried more analytical/arithmetical items (puzzles, blood relations, directions) alongside critical-reasoning passages. All patterns are paraphrased; no actual question or passage is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: Op-ed style passage (≈450 words) on a public-policy or legal theme; 'main idea / central argument' with distractors that are partial, extreme or contrary
Best summary or most appropriate title for the passage; wrong titles are too narrow (one example) or too broad/extreme
What can be inferred from the passage or from a specific statement/example in it; distractors overreach or contradict
What the author would agree with / what a character's remark implies; tests reading of stance rather than literal detail
Meaning of a word as used in the passage; distractors include the word's other (literal or unrelated) senses
Meaning of an idiom or figurative phrase used in the passage
Tone/attitude of the author, options pairing close adjectives (concerned vs indignant, ironic vs mournful)
Primary purpose of the passage or a paragraph (to propose, critique, compare, examine both sides)
Fill-in or correct-usage item set inside a passage sentence: subject–verb agreement with 'along with/neither…nor', tense
Passage on a national political event (election, appointment, census) followed by a question on the related constitutional office or Article
Passage on a national initiative, security operation or commemoration; question on its background facts
Passage on an international summit or grouping (G20, COP, BRICS); question on host, membership or presidency
Passage on an international organisation, treaty or leader; question on headquarters, origin or office-holder
Passage on GST, RBI policy or the Budget; question on the constitutional/statutory basis (Article, committee composition)
Passage on an economic reform (tax code, labour codes); question on its scope or key numbers
Passage on a space mission or science Nobel; question on the agency, partner or discovery
Passage on climate negotiations or conservation; question on the agreement's goals or programme history
Passage on a sporting event or award; question on venue, winner or the awarding body
Passage on a Supreme Court reference/judgment or new criminal law; question on the constitutional provision or statute replaced
Passage on a newly enacted or amended statute (data protection, waqf, online gaming); question on its year, name or core prohibition
Principle of negligence (duty, breach, foreseeability) applied to facts where the defendant took reasonable care or the plaintiff's own conduct caused harm
Strict/absolute liability and defences (volenti, act of God, rescue doctrine) applied to a fact situation
Vicarious liability: was the employee acting in the course of employment or on a 'frolic of his own'?
Offer/acceptance and communication rules (postal acceptance, revocation timing, silence)
Consideration, capacity (minor's agreement void ab initio) and free consent applied to facts
Frustration, void agreements and remoteness of damages (loss not in parties' contemplation)
Property offences under the BNS—theft, extortion, cheating—where one ingredient (taking out of possession, fear of injury, dishonest inducement) decides the case
General exceptions: private defence limits, child below seven, mistake of fact in good faith
Joint liability/common intention and the gradation of homicide offences
Article 14/15 reasonable classification (intelligible differentia and rational nexus) applied to a State measure
Article 19 freedoms and whether a restriction falls within the permitted grounds and is reasonable/proportionate
Article 20 protections (ex post facto penalty, self-incrimination) applied to facts
IP principles: idea–expression dichotomy in copyright, deceptive similarity in trademarks
Special statutes (Consumer Protection Act, RTI etc.): does the person fall within the statutory definition?
Environmental principles (polluter pays, precautionary principle) or diplomatic immunity applied to facts
Short argument passage; identify the assumption on which the conclusion depends
What can most reasonably be inferred from data or claims in the passage
Which option most weakens a causal claim (confounder, alternative explanation, survivorship)
Which option most strengthens a claim (control group, ruling out alternatives)
Categorical statements; which conclusion must be true (syllogistic)
Identify the main conclusion of an argument, or the conclusion best supported by the passage
Analogy between legal/institutional terms or role pairs
Blood relations and direction-sense puzzles (more frequent in 2026)
Ordering/scheduling puzzles: comparisons of rank, days or experience
Caselet with percentages of sub-groups (applications, cases); compute totals or shares
Table of figures for several units; aggregate rates where averaging percentages is the trap
Ratio changes when a group is added or removed
Averages with correction or replacement of a member
Partnership: profit shared in proportion to capital × time
Mark-up/discount and successive sale profit-loss chains
Compound interest repayment or mensuration cost problems (carpeting, fencing)

resources.notes: The Consortium publishes previous CLAT UG question papers with answer keys, provisional and final answer keys after each exam, and sample papers/preparation material for registered candidates on consortiumofnlus.ac.in.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"A courtroom is often imagined as a contest of eloquence, in which the advocate with the finest speech carries the day. The reality is quieter. Most cases are won or lost long before anyone stands up, in the patient assembling of documents, the checking of dates and the anticipation of the other side's best argument. A brilliant speech built on a careless file is a house on sand; a modest speech built on a meticulous file will usually stand."

Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Careful preparation matters more to the outcome of a case than courtroom eloquence.
Most cases are decided by the eloquence of the advocates.
Advocates should avoid making speeches in court.
Judges are unaffected by the quality of advocacy.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the popular image of eloquence with the 'quieter' reality that cases are decided by preparation; the house-on-sand image reinforces this.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"When the village school introduced a midday meal, attendance rose within a single term. Teachers noticed something else: afternoon lessons, once a struggle against drowsy and distracted children, became the most productive part of the day. The headmistress, who had spent years petitioning for more textbooks, remarked that she had been asking for the wrong thing first."

What can most reasonably be inferred from the headmistress's remark?
options: She regretted that the midday meal had been introduced.
She thought textbooks were of no educational value.
She came to believe that children's nutrition was a more urgent need than additional textbooks.
She believed attendance had fallen because of the meal scheme.
questions.explanation: Seeing the gains from the meal, she said she had been 'asking for the wrong thing first' — implying food should have been the priority, not that books are useless.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The committee's report was so equivocal that both the supporters and the opponents of the project claimed it as a vindication of their views. Each side quoted the sentences that suited it and ignored the rest."

As used in the passage, 'equivocal' most nearly means:
options: highly technical
strongly critical
open to more than one interpretation
unusually brief
questions.explanation: Because both opposing sides could claim the report supported them, it must have been ambiguous — open to more than one interpretation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Every few years, a new app promises to make us productive at last. It will sort our emails, schedule our hours and remind us, with gentle chimes, of everything we have not done. We download it with hope, configure it with care and abandon it within the month—only to greet its successor with the same bright faith. Perhaps the problem was never the software."

The tone of the passage is best described as:
options: angry and accusatory
gently ironic
mournful
neutral and technical
questions.explanation: The cycle of 'bright faith' and abandonment, and the closing hint that the problem lies with us, are wry and mildly mocking — gentle irony, not anger or grief.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Rivers rarely respect the boundaries drawn across them. A dam built upstream changes not only how much water reaches the downstream country but when it arrives and how much silt it carries. Treaties that divide water by volume alone may therefore leave the downstream party poorer even when every promised litre is delivered on time."

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: A water-sharing treaty can be fully complied with and still disadvantage the downstream country.
Water-sharing treaties should not mention volumes of water at all.
Silt is harmful to downstream agriculture.
Upstream countries usually violate water-sharing treaties.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the downstream party may be poorer 'even when every promised litre is delivered', because timing and silt also matter. The passage does not allege violations or say silt is harmful.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Translation of laws into regional languages is often treated as a courtesy. It is better seen as a condition of legitimacy. A citizen who cannot read the rules that bind her must rely on intermediaries to tell her what they mean, and every intermediary is a possible point of error or exploitation. The rule of law presupposes that the law can be known by those it governs."

The author's central argument is that:
options: intermediaries always exploit citizens who do not read the law
making laws available in languages people understand is essential to the rule of law
translation of laws is a courtesy extended by the state
laws should be drafted only in regional languages
questions.explanation: The author rejects the 'courtesy' framing and argues that knowability of the law, through translation, is a condition of legitimacy and of the rule of law. 'Always exploit' overstates the passage's 'possible point of error'.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"After months of acrimonious negotiations, marked by walk-outs and public accusations, the two unions finally signed a joint agreement."

The word 'acrimonious' is closest in meaning to:
options: friendly
bitter
lengthy
secret
questions.explanation: Walk-outs and public accusations indicate hostility; 'acrimonious' means bitter or angry.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Neither the petitioner nor his lawyers ____ present when the matter was called out, and the bench adjourned the hearing."

Choose the word that correctly fills the blank.
options: is
was
were
has been
questions.explanation: With 'neither…nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'lawyers' (plural), and the sentence is in the past tense: 'were'.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Some argue that the monuments of a fallen regime should be torn down; others, that they should stand untouched as history. A third path deserves more attention: leave the statue in place, but place beside it an honest account of what its subject did. Removal can erase memory, and silence can glorify; explanation does neither."

The primary purpose of the passage is to:
options: criticise historians for ignoring monuments
argue that all monuments of fallen regimes must be destroyed
describe the history of a particular statue
propose an alternative to two opposing approaches
questions.explanation: The author sets out two positions and then offers 'a third path' — contextual explanation — as preferable to both.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The new bus lanes cut journey times for passengers by a fifth in their first year. Shopkeepers on the route, who had protested that the loss of parking would ruin them, reported footfall roughly unchanged. One of them admitted that most of his customers had always arrived on foot or by bus; he had simply never asked them."

The shopkeeper's admission suggests that the protests against the bus lanes were based on:
options: complaints from bus passengers
a decline in footfall after the lanes opened
an untested assumption about how customers travelled
accurate data on customers' parking habits
questions.explanation: He 'had simply never asked' his customers, so the fear of losing parking rested on an assumption that turned out to be wrong; footfall was unchanged.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Courts often say that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done. The second half of the phrase is sometimes mistaken for a concern with appearances. It is more than that. A decision reached fairly but in secret cannot be checked; the public must take its fairness on trust. Openness is what converts a private assurance of fairness into a public, verifiable fact."

Which of the following best summarises the passage?
options: All court proceedings must be broadcast live.
Open justice matters because it allows the fairness of decisions to be verified rather than merely assumed.
Decisions made in secret are always unfair.
Courts care more about how their decisions look than about whether they are fair.
questions.explanation: The author argues 'seen to be done' is not about appearances but about verifiability. The passage does not say secret decisions are always unfair — only that their fairness cannot be checked.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The minister's statement was a masterpiece of obfuscation: it ran to four pages, used every available technical term, and left readers no clearer about whether the scheme would continue."

As used here, 'obfuscation' means:
options: admitting a mistake
making something deliberately unclear
expressing open anger
giving a precise explanation
questions.explanation: The statement was long and technical yet left readers 'no clearer' — it obscured the matter, which is what obfuscation means.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"On 24 November 2025, Justice Surya Kant took the oath as the 53rd Chief Justice of India, succeeding Justice B. R. Gavai. The oath was administered at Rashtrapati Bhavan. Under the Constitution, judges of the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice, are appointed by the President."

Which Article of the Constitution of India provides for the appointment of judges of the Supreme Court by the President?
options: Article 143
Article 217
Article 32
Article 124
questions.explanation: Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court and, in clause (2), provides for appointment of its judges by the President. Article 217 concerns High Court judges, Article 32 the right to constitutional remedies, and Article 143 the President's advisory reference.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Three new criminal laws—the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam—came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing colonial-era statutes that had governed criminal justice in India for well over a century."

Which statute did the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 replace?
options: The Indian Penal Code, 1860
The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
The Indian Evidence Act, 1872
questions.explanation: The BSA replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; the BNS replaced the IPC and the BNSS replaced the CrPC.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In September 2025 the GST Council approved a major rationalisation of rates, collapsing most goods into two principal slabs of 5% and 18%, with a separate higher rate for a small list of luxury and 'sin' goods. The changes took effect from 22 September 2025."

The GST Council is a constitutional body established under which Article?
options: Article 112
Article 280
Article 279A
Article 246A
questions.explanation: Article 279A (inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016) provides for the GST Council. Article 246A gives the power to levy GST, Article 280 deals with the Finance Commission, and Article 112 with the Annual Financial Statement (Budget).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In mid-2025, Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla flew to the International Space Station aboard the Axiom-4 mission, becoming the first Indian to visit the ISS and only the second Indian to travel to space. His experience is expected to inform ISRO's human spaceflight programme."

Who was the first Indian to travel to space?
options: Rakesh Sharma
Sunita Williams
Kalpana Chawla
Ravish Malhotra
questions.explanation: Rakesh Sharma flew aboard the Soviet Soyuz T-11 to the Salyut 7 station in 1984. Kalpana Chawla was an American astronaut of Indian origin; Ravish Malhotra was Sharma's backup.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"NISAR, an Earth-observation satellite carrying synthetic aperture radar in two frequency bands, was launched in July 2025 on a GSLV rocket from Sriharikota. It is designed to map changes in land and ice surfaces, helping to track earthquakes, landslides and glaciers."

NISAR is a joint mission of ISRO and which agency?
options: Roscosmos
NASA
ESA
JAXA
questions.explanation: NISAR stands for NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar; it is a collaboration between ISRO and the US agency NASA.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Following the terror attack at Pahalgam in April 2025, India announced that it would hold the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan 'in abeyance'. The treaty, signed in 1960, allocates the waters of the eastern rivers to India and the western rivers largely to Pakistan."

The Indus Waters Treaty was signed with the mediation of which institution?
options: The World Bank
The United Nations Security Council
The Commonwealth Secretariat
The International Court of Justice
questions.explanation: The 1960 treaty was brokered by the World Bank (then the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development), which is also a signatory for certain provisions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The 2025 UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) was held in Belém, at the edge of the Amazon, ten years after the adoption of the Paris Agreement. Negotiators reviewed how far national pledges fall short of the agreement's temperature goals."

In which country is Belém, the host city of COP30, located?
options: Peru
Brazil
Colombia
Argentina
questions.explanation: Belém is the capital of the state of Pará in northern Brazil, at the mouth of the Amazon.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"South Africa hosted the G20 Leaders' Summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, the first G20 summit held on the African continent. The African Union had been admitted as a permanent member of the G20 two years earlier."

The African Union became a permanent member of the G20 at the summit hosted by which country?
options: Japan
Indonesia
India
Brazil
questions.explanation: The AU was admitted as a permanent member at the New Delhi G20 Summit under India's presidency in September 2023.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In September 2025, C. P. Radhakrishnan was elected Vice-President of India after the previous incumbent resigned in July citing health reasons. Apart from his constitutional role as Vice-President, he also presides over one House of Parliament."

By virtue of his office, the Vice-President of India is the:
options: Chairman of the NITI Aayog
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Head of the Election Commission
ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: Article 64 makes the Vice-President the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States (Rajya Sabha).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"India's next population census, delayed from 2021, is scheduled with a reference date of 1 March 2027 for most of the country. It will be the first census conducted largely through digital means and will also enumerate caste."

Under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, 'Census' is a subject in the:
options: Residuary powers only
Concurrent List
Union List
State List
questions.explanation: Census is Entry 69 of List I (Union List), so Parliament has exclusive power to legislate on it.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In November 2025 the Union government notified the rules under India's personal data protection law, setting out phased timelines for consent managers, breach reporting and the functioning of the Data Protection Board of India."

In which year was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, under which these rules were framed, enacted?
questions.explanation: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed by Parliament and received Presidential assent in August 2023; the rules followed in November 2025.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In November 2025 India's women's team won the ICC Women's Cricket World Cup for the first time, defeating South Africa in the final at Navi Mumbai. The International Cricket Council, which organises the tournament, is the global governing body of the sport."

Where is the headquarters of the International Cricket Council?
options: Melbourne
Mumbai
London
Dubai
questions.explanation: The ICC moved its headquarters from Lord's, London, to Dubai in 2005, where it remains.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado for her work promoting democratic rights. Unlike the other Nobel prizes, which are presented in Stockholm, the Peace Prize is presented in a different city."

In which city is the Nobel Peace Prize presented?
options: Oslo
Copenhagen
Helsinki
Geneva
questions.explanation: In accordance with Alfred Nobel's will, the Peace Prize is awarded by the Norwegian Nobel Committee and presented in Oslo.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee meets at least four times a year to set the policy repo rate, with the objective of keeping consumer price inflation at a target of 4% within a tolerance band of ±2 percentage points."

How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee have?
options: Five
Seven
Six
Nine
questions.explanation: Under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934, the MPC has six members: the Governor (chair), a Deputy Governor, one RBI officer and three external members appointed by the Centre.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Each year the Union Budget is presented to Parliament as the 'Annual Financial Statement', setting out the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for the coming financial year. Since 2017 it has been presented on 1 February."

The Annual Financial Statement is laid before Parliament under which Article of the Constitution?
options: Article 110
Article 112
Article 280
Article 265
questions.explanation: Article 112 requires the President to cause the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before both Houses. Article 110 defines Money Bills, Article 265 bars tax without authority of law, and Article 280 concerns the Finance Commission.

questions.question:
Principle: A person who brings onto his land, for his own purposes, something likely to do mischief if it escapes is liable for the damage naturally caused by its escape, even if he was not negligent. The liability does not arise where the escape is caused by an act of God, i.e. an extraordinary natural event that no human foresight could have guarded against.

Facts: Rakesh stores large quantities of industrial chemicals in a tank on his factory premises. Owing to a crack caused by ordinary wear, chemicals leak into Meena's adjoining farm and destroy her crop. Rakesh shows that he had inspected the tank regularly and had taken every reasonable care.

Is Rakesh liable to Meena?
options: Yes, but only if Meena proves that Rakesh intended the leak.
Yes, because liability under the principle does not depend on negligence, and ordinary wear is not an act of God.
No, because the leak was an act of God.
No, because he took every reasonable care.
questions.explanation: The principle imposes liability for escape 'even if he was not negligent'. A crack from ordinary wear is not an extraordinary natural event, so the act-of-God exception does not apply; intent is irrelevant.

questions.question:
Principle: A person is liable in negligence if he owes a duty of care to another, breaches that duty, and the breach causes damage to that other person. A person who voluntarily and knowingly accepts a risk cannot later complain of harm arising from that very risk.

Facts: Arjun buys a ticket to watch a cricket match from the stands. During the match a batsman hits a six and the ball strikes Arjun, injuring him. The stadium's boundary and stands meet the usual safety standards for cricket grounds.

Can Arjun recover damages from the stadium?
options: Yes, because the batsman intended to hit the ball out of the ground.
No, because Arjun did not pay enough for his ticket.
Yes, because the stadium owes a duty of care to every ticket-holder.
No, because a spectator at a cricket match voluntarily accepts the ordinary risk of being hit by the ball.
questions.explanation: Being struck by a six is an ordinary, known risk of watching cricket from the stands, and the stadium met usual standards, so there is no breach and the voluntary-acceptance principle bars the claim. Ticket price is irrelevant.

questions.question:
Principle: An employer is vicariously liable for a wrong committed by an employee in the course of employment, that is, while doing the work he was employed to do, even if done in an unauthorised manner. The employer is not liable for acts done by the employee on a 'frolic of his own', unconnected with his employment.

Facts: Sunil, a delivery driver for QuickMart, is told to drive only on main roads. To save time while delivering a parcel, he takes a narrow lane and negligently knocks down a pedestrian, Kavya.

Is QuickMart liable to Kavya?
options: Yes, because Sunil was doing his job of delivering, though in an unauthorised manner.
No, because Sunil was on a frolic of his own.
Yes, but only if QuickMart owned the lane.
No, because Sunil disobeyed the instruction to use main roads.
questions.explanation: Sunil was delivering a parcel — the very work he was employed to do — only by a forbidden route. That is an unauthorised manner of doing authorised work, not a frolic of his own, so QuickMart is vicariously liable.

questions.question:
Principle: An agreement made without consideration is void, unless it is in writing and registered and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other.

Facts: Out of love for his daughter Priya, Mohan promises in a written and registered document to give her ₹5 lakh. Later he refuses to pay.

Can Priya enforce the promise?
options: Yes, but only if Priya proves she relied on the promise.
No, because Priya gave no consideration.
No, because promises to family members are never enforceable.
Yes, because the promise is in writing, registered and made out of natural love and affection to a near relative.
questions.explanation: Though there is no consideration, the stated exception applies: written, registered, out of natural love and affection, between near relatives (father and daughter). So the agreement is enforceable.

questions.question:
Principle: An acceptance must be communicated to the offeror. Mere silence of the offeree does not amount to acceptance, even if the offeror says that silence will be treated as acceptance.

Facts: Farid writes to Gita: 'I offer to buy your old car for ₹2 lakh. If I hear nothing from you by Friday, I shall consider the car mine.' Gita does not reply. On Saturday Farid demands the car.

Is there a binding contract?
options: Yes, because Gita did not reject the offer before Friday.
No, because Gita's silence does not amount to acceptance.
No, because the price offered was too low.
Yes, because Farid clearly stated that silence would be acceptance.
questions.explanation: The principle says silence is not acceptance even if the offeror declares it will be. Gita never communicated acceptance, so there is no contract. Adequacy of price is irrelevant.

questions.question:
Principle: A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible or unlawful through no fault of the promisor, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful.

Facts: A singer, Lata, contracts with an event company to perform at a concert on 10 March. On 8 March the district authorities lawfully prohibit all public gatherings in the city because of an epidemic. The concert cannot take place. The company sues Lata for breach.

Which is correct?
options: The contract was void from the beginning.
Lata is liable because she should have performed in another city.
The contract became void when the performance became unlawful, so Lata is not liable.
Lata is liable because she did not perform on 10 March.
questions.explanation: After the contract was made, performance became unlawful through no fault of Lata, so the contract became void at that point; it was valid when made, so it was not void from the start.

questions.question:
Principle: Whoever intentionally takes dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moving that property in order to such taking, commits theft. 'Dishonestly' means with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another.

Facts: Neha borrows her friend Ritu's bicycle with Ritu's permission for an afternoon. In the evening, instead of returning it, Neha sells it and keeps the money.

Has Neha committed theft?
options: No, because a bicycle is not movable property.
Yes, because she caused wrongful loss to Ritu.
No, because the bicycle was not taken out of Ritu's possession without her consent.
Yes, because she sold the bicycle dishonestly.
questions.explanation: Theft requires taking out of another's possession without consent. Neha obtained possession with Ritu's consent; her later dishonest sale may be another offence (such as criminal breach of trust or misappropriation), but on the stated principle it is not theft.

questions.question:
Principle: Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence. The right of private defence of the body arises as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises, and it does not extend to inflicting more harm than is necessary for the purpose of defence. The right ends once the apprehension of danger ceases.

Facts: Vikram attacks Anil with a stick. Anil snatches the stick, and Vikram, now unarmed, turns and runs away. Anil chases him for 200 metres and beats him with the stick, fracturing his arm.

Can Anil claim the right of private defence?
options: Yes, because Anil used Vikram's own stick.
No, because the danger had ceased when Vikram ran away unarmed, so the right had ended.
No, because private defence is never available against an attack with a stick.
Yes, because Vikram was the original aggressor.
questions.explanation: Once Vikram was disarmed and fleeing, there was no continuing apprehension of danger, so the right had ended; the later beating was retaliation, not defence.

questions.question:
Principle: Nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age. Nothing is an offence which is done by a child above seven and under twelve years of age who has not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of the act.

Facts: Six-year-old Rohan picks up a valuable pen from a shop counter and walks out with it, knowing that his parents had not paid for it.

Has Rohan committed an offence?
options: Yes, if he understood the nature of his act.
Yes, because he knew the pen had not been paid for.
No, but only if the pen is returned.
No, because nothing done by a child under seven is an offence.
questions.explanation: Under the first limb, any act of a child under seven is not an offence, regardless of understanding. The maturity test applies only to children between seven and twelve.

questions.question:
Principle: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws. A law that classifies persons is valid only if (i) the classification is based on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those grouped together from others, and (ii) the differentia has a rational relation to the object of the law.

Facts: To reduce road accidents caused by inexperience, a State law requires drivers who obtained their licence less than one year ago to display a 'New Driver' sticker. It does not apply to drivers with longer experience.

Is the law likely to be valid under the principle?
options: Yes, because the State can make any classification it chooses.
Yes, because driving experience is an intelligible differentia rationally connected to the object of reducing accidents caused by inexperience.
No, because the law classifies people at all.
No, because all drivers must be treated identically.
questions.explanation: The principle permits classification meeting both tests. 'Licensed less than a year' is an intelligible basis and is rationally linked to reducing accidents by inexperienced drivers. The principle does not demand identical treatment, nor allow arbitrary classification.

questions.question:
Principle: Article 20(1): No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.

Facts: In January, Deepak sold loose cigarettes near a school, which was then punishable with a fine of ₹200. In March, the law was amended to raise the fine to ₹2,000. In April, Deepak was convicted for the January sale.

What is the maximum fine that can lawfully be imposed on Deepak?
options: No fine, because the law was amended
questions.explanation: Article 20(1) bars a penalty greater than that under the law in force when the offence was committed. In January the fine was ₹200, so that is the maximum; the act was an offence at the time, so he can still be punished.

questions.question:
Principle: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees to all citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression. Under Article 19(2), the State may impose reasonable restrictions on this right only in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Facts: A State passes a law banning all newspapers from criticising the economic policies of the State government, on the ground that such criticism 'lowers investor confidence'.

Is the law valid?
options: Yes, because newspapers are not citizens.
No, because freedom of speech can never be restricted.
No, because 'investor confidence' is not among the grounds on which speech may be restricted.
Yes, because the State has an interest in protecting its economy.
questions.explanation: Restrictions are allowed 'only' on the listed grounds; protecting investor confidence is not one of them. The option that speech can never be restricted contradicts Article 19(2).

questions.question:
Principle: Copyright protects the original expression of an idea, not the idea itself. Copying the idea without copying its expression does not infringe copyright.

Facts: Author A writes a novel about a young girl who disguises herself as a boy to join a cricket team. Author B, after reading it, writes a completely different story, with different characters, dialogue, settings and plot development, about a girl who disguises herself as a boy to join a football team.

Has B infringed A's copyright?
options: No, because B has used only the idea and not A's expression of it.
Yes, because B read A's novel before writing.
Yes, because both stories involve a girl disguised as a boy.
No, because football is a different sport from cricket.
questions.explanation: Only the general idea (a girl disguised as a boy to play a sport) is shared; characters, dialogue, settings and plot are B's own. Ideas are not protected, so there is no infringement.

questions.question:
Principle: Under the 'polluter pays' principle, the person or entity responsible for causing environmental damage must bear the cost of remedying it, including restoring the environment and compensating victims, irrespective of whether the activity was otherwise lawful.

Facts: A licensed tannery discharges effluents within permitted limits, but over years the effluents accumulate and contaminate groundwater in nearby villages. The tannery argues that it held a valid licence and complied with its conditions.

Who must bear the cost of cleaning the groundwater?
options: The tannery, because it caused the damage, even though it acted lawfully.
The State, because it granted the licence.
No one, because the discharges were within permitted limits.
The villagers, because they used the groundwater.
questions.explanation: The principle makes the polluter pay 'irrespective of whether the activity was otherwise lawful'. The tannery caused the contamination, so it bears the cost.

questions.question:
Principle: A diplomatic agent enjoys immunity from the criminal jurisdiction of the receiving State. This immunity may be waived only by the sending State, and the waiver must be express.

Facts: A diplomat of Country X posted in New Delhi causes a road accident in which a pedestrian is injured. The police wish to prosecute him. Country X has made no statement about waiving his immunity.

Can the diplomat be prosecuted in India?
options: Yes, because the pedestrian suffered serious injury.
Yes, because Country X's silence amounts to a waiver.
Yes, because the accident occurred on Indian territory.
No, because he enjoys immunity from criminal jurisdiction and Country X has not expressly waived it.
questions.explanation: Immunity from the receiving State's criminal jurisdiction applies regardless of where the act occurred or how serious it is, and waiver must be express — silence is not enough. So he cannot be prosecuted in India unless X expressly waives immunity.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The city should replace its diesel buses with electric buses. Electric buses produce no tailpipe emissions, so air quality along bus routes will improve."

The argument assumes that:
options: diesel buses contribute meaningfully to air pollution along bus routes
electricity in the city is generated only from renewable sources
electric buses are cheaper to buy than diesel buses
all residents of the city use buses
questions.explanation: For removing bus tailpipe emissions to improve air quality, diesel buses must be a meaningful source of that pollution. Cost, universal ridership and the energy mix are not needed for this conclusion about air along routes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Students who take music lessons score higher in mathematics than those who do not. Therefore, music lessons improve mathematical ability."

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
options: Some famous mathematicians were also skilled musicians.
Music involves rhythm, which has a mathematical structure.
Music lessons are offered in most urban schools.
Families who can afford music lessons also tend to pay for extra mathematics tuition.
questions.explanation: If music students also get more maths tuition, the higher scores may be caused by that tuition (or family resources), not music — an alternative explanation that weakens the causal claim.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"After the town installed CCTV cameras in its market, reported thefts in the market fell by 30% within a year. The council concludes that the cameras deterred thieves."

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the council's conclusion?
options: Thefts in neighbouring streets without cameras rose during the year.
The council spent a large sum on installing the cameras.
Many shopkeepers support the use of cameras.
Reported thefts in comparable markets without cameras did not fall over the same period.
questions.explanation: A control comparison showing no decline elsewhere rules out a general trend as the cause. A rise in neighbouring streets suggests displacement rather than deterrence; cost and opinion are irrelevant.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"All members of the debating club are students of the law faculty. Some students of the law faculty are members of the moot court society. No member of the moot court society is a member of the drama club."

Which of the following must be true?
options: Some students of the law faculty are not members of the drama club.
No member of the debating club is a member of the drama club.
All students of the law faculty are members of the debating club.
Some members of the debating club are members of the moot court society.
questions.explanation: Some law students are in the moot court society, and no moot court member is in the drama club, so those law students are not in the drama club. The other options do not follow: debating-club members may or may not overlap with the moot court or drama club.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Notice: From next month, the library will close at 6 pm instead of 9 pm on weekdays to reduce electricity costs. Students who need to study late may use the 24-hour reading room in the hostel."

Which of the following is an assumption underlying the notice?
options: All students live in the hostel.
Keeping the library open in the evenings adds noticeably to electricity costs.
The hostel reading room has more books than the library.
Students do not study after 6 pm.
questions.explanation: Closing early 'to reduce electricity costs' presupposes that evening opening consumes significant electricity. The notice offers an alternative to late-studying students, so it does not assume no one studies after 6 pm.

questions.question: Choose the pair that has the same relationship as 'Legislature : Enact'.
options: Executive : Debate
Judiciary : Adjudicate
Lawyer : Legislate
Police : Sentence
questions.explanation: A legislature's function is to enact laws; likewise the judiciary's function is to adjudicate. Debate is not the executive's defining function, lawyers do not legislate, and police do not sentence.

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

P is the brother of Q. Q is the daughter of R. S is the father of R. T is the mother of P.

How is S related to T?
options: S is T's father or father-in-law
S is T's brother
S is T's son
S is T's husband
questions.explanation: P and Q are siblings, children of R; T is P's mother, so T is the mother of R's children. R's gender is not given: if R is the mother, R = T and S is T's father; if R is the father, T is R's wife and S is T's father-in-law. Hence 'father or father-in-law' is the only option that must be true.

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

From her house, Asha walks 5 km north, turns right and walks 3 km, turns right again and walks 9 km, and then turns left and walks 3 km.

How far, and in which direction, is she from her house?
options: 4 km south
6 km east
10 km south-east
√52 km (about 7.2 km) to the south-east
questions.explanation: Net north–south: +5 − 9 = −4 (4 km south). Net east–west: right from north = east 3 km; after turning right twice she faces south, then a left turn faces east, another 3 km: 6 km east. Distance = √(4² + 6²) = √52 ≈ 7.2 km, south-east.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In the last five years, the number of law graduates in the state has doubled, while the number of litigation cases filed has risen by only 10%. Young lawyers report that it has become harder to find paid work in litigation."

Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred?
options: Litigation cases will decrease in the next five years.
Most law graduates do not want to work in litigation.
The quality of legal education has declined.
Competition among lawyers for litigation work has probably increased.
questions.explanation: The supply of graduates grew much faster than litigation work, consistent with greater competition, which matches young lawyers' reports. The other options go beyond the information.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"A four-day working week will increase productivity, because rested employees work more efficiently."

Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the claim?
options: Some countries are considering a four-day week.
Employees in a pilot study said they preferred a four-day week.
Firms that tried a four-day week found that employees worked longer daily hours and reported more fatigue, with output unchanged.
Productivity has risen in many sectors over the last decade.
questions.explanation: The claim rests on employees being better rested. Evidence that they became more fatigued and output did not rise undercuts both the premise and the conclusion.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Fines for littering have existed in the city for twenty years, yet streets remain dirty. Surveys show that fewer than one in a hundred littering incidents is ever penalised. In neighbouring cities where enforcement is regular, streets are visibly cleaner even though the fines are smaller."

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the passage?
options: The certainty of enforcement matters more for deterring littering than the size of the fine.
Residents of the city do not care about clean streets.
Neighbouring cities have more dustbins.
Fines for littering should be abolished.
questions.explanation: The city has fines but almost no enforcement and dirty streets; neighbours have smaller fines but regular enforcement and cleaner streets. This supports the role of certainty over size of penalty.

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

Five advocates—A, B, C, D and E—are to argue on five consecutive days, Monday to Friday, one per day.
• C argues on Wednesday.
• A argues on some day before B.
• D argues on the day immediately after B.
• E does not argue on Monday.

Who argues on Monday?
options: D
E
B
A
questions.explanation: C is on Wednesday, so B–D (consecutive) must be Mon–Tue or Thu–Fri. If B were Monday, A could not be before B. So B = Thu, D = Fri. A and E take Mon and Tue; E is not on Monday, so A = Monday, E = Tuesday.

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

A district court disposed of 2,400 cases in 2025. Of these, 40% were civil cases and the rest criminal. Of the civil cases, 25% were settled through mediation; of the criminal cases, 10% were compounded (settled by compromise).

How many cases in all were settled through mediation or compounding?
questions.explanation: Civil = 960, mediated = 240. Criminal = 1,440, compounded = 144. Total = 240 + 144 = 384.

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

A law school has 600 students across five years. Years 1 to 5 have 140, 130, 120, 110 and 100 students respectively. In each year, 45% of students are women, except Year 5, where 50% are women.

What percentage of all students in the school are women (to one decimal place)?

Read the information and answer the question.

The average score of 40 students in a moot court qualifying round was 62. It was later found that one student's score had been entered as 84 instead of 48.

What is the correct average?

Read the information and answer the question.

Three partners, X, Y and Z, invest ₹40,000, ₹60,000 and ₹50,000 respectively in a legal-services start-up. X withdraws his entire investment after 6 months, while Y and Z stay for the full year. Annual profit of ₹1,30,000 is shared in proportion to (capital × time).

What is Z's share?

Read the information and answer the question.

A bookseller buys law textbooks at ₹800 each and marks them up by 25%. During a sale he offers a 10% discount on the marked price.

What is his profit percentage on each textbook sold during the sale?
questions.explanation: Marked price = ₹1,000; sale price = ₹900. Profit = ₹100 on ₹800 = 12.5%.

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

A litigant borrows ₹50,000 to pay legal fees at 10% per annum compound interest, compounded annually. At the end of the first year she repays ₹25,000.

How much must she pay at the end of the second year to clear the loan completely?
questions.explanation: After year 1: 50,000 × 1.1 = 55,000; after repaying 25,000, balance 30,000. After year 2: 30,000 × 1.1 = ₹33,000.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Nearly three of every four prisoners in India's jails are undertrials—people who have not been convicted of anything. Many are poor, cannot furnish bail, and remain in custody for longer than the sentence they would receive if found guilty. The law already recognises the problem: an undertrial who has spent half of the maximum term prescribed for the alleged offence is entitled to be considered for release. Yet the provision is applied unevenly, because it depends on someone—a jail officer, a legal-aid lawyer, a judge—noticing that the threshold has been crossed. A right that must be discovered before it can be claimed is, for most prisoners, a right that does not exist."

Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Most undertrial prisoners are eventually found guilty of the offences with which they are charged.
Jail officers deliberately keep eligible undertrials in custody.
The statutory provision for releasing long-detained undertrials should be repealed.
Legal safeguards for undertrials fail in practice when their use depends on someone identifying the prisoners who qualify.
questions.explanation: The passage concedes that the law provides for release but argues it fails because the right must be 'discovered before it can be claimed'. Nothing is said about conviction rates, repeal is the opposite of the author's concern, and no deliberate misconduct by officers is alleged.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"When two neighbours quarrel over a boundary wall, a court can decide who owns the disputed strip of land, but it cannot make them neighbours again. Mediation, which asks the parties to craft their own settlement with the help of a neutral person, aims at something courts rarely attempt: a resolution both sides can live with afterwards. The Mediation Act, 2023 gave this process a statutory framework in India. Critics worry that weaker parties, unable to afford a long trial, may be pressured into unfair compromises. The answer, supporters argue, is not to abandon mediation but to ensure that walking away from it remains a genuine option."

Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: How Courts Decide Boundary Disputes
Beyond Winning and Losing: The Promise and Limits of Mediation
Why Mediation Should Replace the Courts
The Mediation Act, 2023: A Clause-by-Clause Guide
questions.explanation: The passage presents mediation's aim (a settlement both sides can live with), a criticism (pressure on weaker parties) and a response—promise and limits. The boundary dispute is only an opening example; the Act is mentioned once; replacing courts is never proposed.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Lenders increasingly decide who gets a loan using models trained on past repayment data. The appeal is obvious: a model is consistent, fast and immune to a loan officer's bad mood. But a model learns from history, and history is not neutral. If, in the past, women rarely held property in their own names, the data contain few successful women borrowers with collateral, and the model learns to treat applicants who resemble them as risky. The model has never been told anyone's gender; it simply finds proxies, such as the absence of a property record, that track gender closely."

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Property records are unreliable predictors of loan repayment.
Women are inherently riskier borrowers than men.
A lending model can reproduce past exclusion even if gender is never one of its inputs.
Lenders deliberately programme their models to discriminate against women.
questions.explanation: The passage says the model 'has never been told anyone's gender' yet uses proxies that track it, so it can replicate historical exclusion. It attributes the pattern to history, not to women's riskiness or to deliberate programming, and it does not question the reliability of property records.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Ahmedabad's heat action plan, prepared after a deadly heatwave in 2010, did not rely on sophisticated technology. It relied on telling people early and acting before the first hot day: text-message alerts, drinking-water points at bus stops, hospitals that stocked ice packs and cleared beds in advance rather than after the first deaths. Several other cities later copied the plan's documents almost word for word, but not its routines, and found that a plan which exists only on paper does little when the thermometer climbs."

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Ahmedabad's plan succeeded mainly because of advanced weather-forecasting technology.
The cities that copied Ahmedabad's plan experienced more heatwaves than Ahmedabad.
A heat action plan works only if its measures are actually put in place before extreme heat arrives.
Text-message alerts are the most important element of any heat action plan.
questions.explanation: The contrast between Ahmedabad's routines and the cities that copied only the documents shows that implementation in advance is what matters. The passage says the plan 'did not rely on sophisticated technology'; it does not compare the frequency of heatwaves or rank the alerts above other measures.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"A dissenting judgment changes nothing in the case before the court; the majority's order is carried out regardless. Yet dissents have a way of outliving majorities. In 1976, during the Emergency, Justice H. R. Khanna stood alone in insisting that the right to life could not be suspended, and he paid for it with the Chief Justiceship. Four decades later, a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court expressly overruled the majority in that habeas corpus case and endorsed his reasoning. A dissent, as one judge put it, is an appeal to the intelligence of a future day."

The author would most likely agree that:
options: judges should avoid dissenting in order to preserve the unity of the court
a dissent's value may lie in shaping future law even when it has no effect on the case in which it is written
majority judgments of the Supreme Court are usually overruled within a few decades
Justice Khanna's dissent was immediately adopted by Parliament
questions.explanation: The passage says a dissent changes nothing in the immediate case but can be vindicated later, as Justice Khanna's was. Parliament is not mentioned, the author admires the dissent, and one example does not show that majorities are usually overruled.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Officials were sanguine about the new e-filing portal, predicting that the backlog of pending cases would fall within a year. Lawyers who had used the pilot version were less hopeful: the portal crashed during peak hours and rejected scanned documents above a small size."

As used in the passage, 'sanguine' most nearly means:
options: indifferent
anxious
optimistic
bloodthirsty
questions.explanation: Officials predicted the backlog would fall, and lawyers were 'less hopeful'—so the officials were hopeful, i.e. optimistic. 'Bloodthirsty' plays on the word's root (blood), not its meaning here.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The company won its lawsuit against the former employee, but the three-year battle cost it more in legal fees than the damages it was awarded, and the publicity drove away two major clients. Analysts described the outcome as a pyrrhic victory."

The phrase 'pyrrhic victory', as used in the passage, refers to:
options: a victory obtained through deception
a win achieved at such great cost that it is hardly worth having
a victory that is later overturned on appeal
an unexpected win by the weaker side
questions.explanation: The company won, but the fees exceeded the damages and it lost clients—a win whose cost outweighed its benefit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Every year, lakhs of teenagers move to coaching towns, where days are divided between classes, tests and rank lists. Some flourish. Many others begin to measure their worth by a single number published every Sunday. It would be easy to blame the coaching institutes alone, but they sell what parents buy and what an examination system with very few seats rewards. If we want children to stop treating a rank as a verdict on their lives, the adults around them—parents, schools and policymakers—will have to stop treating it that way first."

The tone of the passage is best described as:
options: detached and purely statistical
concerned and reflective, calling for shared responsibility
celebratory of the competitive spirit of coaching towns
indignant, blaming coaching institutes for the problem
questions.explanation: The author worries about students' self-worth but explicitly declines to blame institutes alone, urging parents, schools and policymakers to change—concerned and reflective. There is no indignation, celebration or statistical detachment.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Some countries have adopted a 'right to disconnect', allowing employees to ignore work calls and messages outside working hours without penalty. Supporters argue that constant availability erodes rest and family life and that only a legal right can protect employees who fear seeming uncommitted. Opponents reply that rigid rules suit factories better than teams spread across time zones, where one person's evening is another's morning. A middle path may lie in requiring firms to agree on response-time norms with their employees, rather than in either a blanket ban or no rule at all."

The primary purpose of the passage is to:
options: explain how workplace messaging applications function
criticise employees who reply to messages late at night
examine the arguments for and against a right to disconnect and suggest a compromise
demand immediate legislation banning all after-hours work messages
questions.explanation: The passage sets out supporters' and opponents' views and ends with 'a middle path'. It rejects a blanket ban, says nothing technical about apps, and does not criticise employees.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Following precedent is sometimes mocked as doing something only because it was done before. But the doctrine serves people who will never enter a courtroom. A landlord and a tenant who know how courts have read a lease can settle their dispute without litigation; a business can draft a contract knowing how its clauses will be interpreted. Precedent's real audience is not the judge but everyone who must arrange their affairs in the shadow of the law. That is also why overruling a long-settled precedent should be rare: the cost falls on people who relied on it."

The author's central argument is that:
options: most disputes between landlords and tenants end up in court
judges follow precedent mainly out of habit
settled precedents should never be overruled
precedent matters chiefly because it lets people plan and settle their affairs predictably, which also justifies caution in overruling it
questions.explanation: The author rebuts the 'habit' mockery by pointing to predictability for people outside court and draws the consequence that overruling should be 'rare'—not never. The landlord example shows disputes settled without litigation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"When a highway cuts through a forest, the animals on either side do not merely lose a strip of land. A tiger population split in two becomes two smaller populations, each more vulnerable to inbreeding and local extinction. On the stretch of National Highway 44 that passes between the Pench and Kanha landscapes in Madhya Pradesh, engineers built a series of animal underpasses beneath an elevated road, and camera traps have since recorded tigers, leopards and deer using them. The cost was considerable, but it bought something no compensation payment could: a forest that still functions as one."

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Highways should never be built near forests.
Tigers generally avoid using man-made structures.
Underpasses eliminate all risks that highways pose to tigers.
The main harm of a road through a forest may lie in dividing animal populations rather than in the land the road occupies.
questions.explanation: The passage says animals 'do not merely lose a strip of land'—fragmentation of populations is the deeper harm. Camera traps show tigers using the underpasses (contradicting the third option); 'all risks' and 'never' overreach.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The committee, along with its two advisers, ____ expected to submit its report before the end of the session, and the Speaker has fixed a date for the debate."

Choose the word that correctly fills the blank.
options: have been
are
is
were
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The committee' (singular); a phrase introduced by 'along with' does not change the number of the subject. The present tense matches 'has fixed', so 'is' is correct.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"After the NDA's victory in the Bihar Assembly election held in November 2025, Nitish Kumar was sworn in as Chief Minister for a record tenth time. The Governor administered the oath of office and secrecy to him and to the members of his council of ministers at a ceremony in Patna."

Under which Article of the Constitution of India is the Chief Minister of a State appointed by the Governor?
options: Article 164
Article 75
Article 154
Article 163
questions.explanation: Article 164(1) provides that the Chief Minister shall be appointed by the Governor and other ministers on the Chief Minister's advice. Article 163 deals with the council of ministers aiding the Governor, 154 with the State's executive power, and 75 with the Union Prime Minister.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The Constitution (One Hundred and Twenty-Ninth Amendment) Bill, 2024, which seeks to enable simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies, was introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2024 and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee. The Bill followed the report of a High-Level Committee on simultaneous elections submitted in March 2024."

Who chaired the High-Level Committee on simultaneous elections?
options: Ram Nath Kovind
Ranjan Gogoi
Arjun Ram Meghwal
Rajiv Kumar
questions.explanation: The High-Level Committee on 'One Nation, One Election', constituted in 2023, was chaired by former President Ram Nath Kovind and submitted its report in March 2024.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In May 2025, the Indian armed forces carried out precision strikes on terrorist infrastructure across the border under 'Operation Sindoor'. The government described the operation as a measured response to a terror attack in which 26 people, most of them tourists, were killed in April 2025."

The terror attack to which Operation Sindoor was a response took place at:
options: Uri
Pulwama
Gulmarg
Pahalgam
questions.explanation: Operation Sindoor (7 May 2025) followed the 22 April 2025 attack near Pahalgam in Jammu and Kashmir. Pulwama (2019) and Uri (2016) were earlier attacks.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"On 7 November 2025, the Government of India launched a year-long commemoration marking 150 years of 'Vande Mataram'. The song, adopted as the National Song, was composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and later became a rallying cry of the freedom struggle."

In which of Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novels did 'Vande Mataram' appear?
options: Kapalkundala
Durgeshnandini
Anandamath
Devi Chaudhurani
questions.explanation: 'Vande Mataram' was included in Bankim Chandra's novel Anandamath (1882). The other three are also his novels, which is what makes them plausible distractors.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"South Africa hosted the G20 Leaders' Summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, the first G20 summit held in Africa. At the end of its presidency, South Africa handed over the rotating presidency of the group for 2026."

Which country holds the G20 presidency in 2026?
options: United States
Brazil
India
United Kingdom
questions.explanation: The G20 presidency passed from South Africa (2025) to the United States for 2026. India held it in 2023 and Brazil in 2024.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In May 2025, the College of Cardinals elected Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost as Pope. Taking the name Leo XIV, he became the first Pope born in the United States and the head of the Catholic Church and the Vatican City State."

Whom did Pope Leo XIV succeed?
options: Pope John XXIII
Pope John Paul II
Pope Francis
Pope Benedict XVI
questions.explanation: Pope Leo XIV was elected after the death of Pope Francis in April 2025. Benedict XVI resigned in 2013 and was succeeded by Francis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala began her second term as Director-General of the World Trade Organization on 1 September 2025, after members reappointed her by consensus. She is the first woman and the first African to lead the organisation, which administers the rules of international trade."

Where is the headquarters of the World Trade Organization?
options: Vienna
Paris
New York
Geneva
questions.explanation: The WTO, established in 1995, is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The Income-tax Act, 2025, which replaces the Income-tax Act, 1961, came into force on 1 April 2026. It simplifies the language of the law and replaces the familiar concepts of 'previous year' and 'assessment year' with a single 'tax year'."

Which Article of the Constitution of India provides that no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law?
options: Article 265
Article 280
Article 112
Article 266
questions.explanation: Article 265 bars any tax except by authority of law. Article 266 deals with the Consolidated Fund, 112 with the Annual Financial Statement, and 280 with the Finance Commission.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"On 21 November 2025, the Government of India brought into force the four Labour Codes—the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. The codes were enacted in 2019 and 2020 to simplify India's labour regulation."

How many existing central labour laws were consolidated into the four Labour Codes?
questions.explanation: The four Labour Codes subsume 29 central labour laws.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Clarke, Michel H. Devoret and John M. Martinis. Their experiments in the 1980s, using superconducting electrical circuits, laid foundations for today's quantum technologies, including superconducting quantum computers."

For which discovery were they awarded the prize?
options: Efficient blue light-emitting diodes
The first observation of gravitational waves
Macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit
Experimental methods that generate attosecond pulses of light
questions.explanation: The 2025 prize cited macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit. Blue LEDs (2014), gravitational waves (2017) and attosecond pulses (2023) were earlier physics prizes.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The UN Climate Change Conference, COP30, met in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025, ten years after the Paris Agreement was adopted. Negotiators reviewed new national climate pledges, which together still fall short of the Agreement's temperature goal."

The Paris Agreement aims to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below how many degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C?
questions.explanation: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement (2015) sets the goal of holding warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In July 2025, 19-year-old Divya Deshmukh won the FIDE Women's World Cup in Batumi, Georgia, defeating a more experienced Indian compatriot in an all-Indian final decided in tie-breaks. The victory also earned her the Grandmaster title."

Whom did Divya Deshmukh defeat in the final?
options: R. Vaishali
D. Harika
Tan Zhongyi
Koneru Humpy
questions.explanation: Divya Deshmukh beat Koneru Humpy in the all-Indian final of the 2025 FIDE Women's World Cup in Batumi.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"In November 2025, a five-judge Constitution Bench gave its opinion on a reference made by the President on whether courts can fix timelines for Governors and the President to act on Bills passed by State Legislatures. The Bench held that such timelines cannot be judicially imposed and that the concept of 'deemed assent' is not permissible."

Under which Article of the Constitution can the President refer a question of law to the Supreme Court for its opinion?
options: Article 32
Article 200
Article 143
Article 131
questions.explanation: Article 143 confers advisory jurisdiction on the Supreme Court on references by the President. Article 200 governs the Governor's assent to Bills, which was the subject of the reference—hence a tempting distractor.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, passed by Parliament in April 2025, changed the composition of waqf boards, the process of registering waqf properties and the powers of survey. The amending Act also renamed the principal law, the Waqf Act, 1995."

What is the new name given to the Waqf Act, 1995 by the 2025 amendment?
options: Central Waqf Council Act, 1995
Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development Act, 1995
Waqf Properties (Registration and Survey) Act, 1995
National Waqf Regulation and Protection Act, 1995
questions.explanation: The 2025 amendment renamed the principal Act the Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development (UMEED) Act, 1995.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 was passed by Parliament in August 2025. It seeks to promote e-sports and online social games while addressing concerns about addiction and financial losses suffered by players."

Which of the following does the Act prohibit?
options: Offering and advertising online money games played for stakes
Organising e-sports tournaments
Online chess and other skill-based social games
All mobile games for users below 18 years
questions.explanation: The Act bans online money games (where users deposit money in expectation of winnings), along with their advertisement and related transactions, while promoting e-sports and social games.

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: A person is liable in negligence if he owes a duty of care to another, breaches that duty by failing to take the care a reasonable person would take in the circumstances, and the breach causes foreseeable harm. A person who has taken all reasonable precautions is not liable.

Facts: A supermarket mops one aisle during business hours and places two large, brightly coloured 'Wet Floor' boards at either end of the aisle. Raj, reading messages on his phone, walks past one board without looking up, slips and breaks his wrist.

Is the supermarket liable to Raj in negligence?
options: No, because it took the precautions a reasonable shop would take to warn customers of the wet floor.
Yes, because the floor should never be mopped during business hours.
No, because Raj was not a paying customer at the time of the fall.
Yes, because a shop owes a duty of care to every customer and Raj was injured on its premises.
questions.explanation: Duty exists, but there is no breach: clearly visible warning boards at both ends are reasonable precautions, and the principle excuses a defendant who took them. Injury on the premises alone does not establish negligence, and nothing suggests Raj was not a customer.

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: An employer is liable for a wrong committed by an employee in the course of employment, including an authorised act done in an unauthorised manner. The employer is not liable where the employee, at the time of the wrong, was acting purely for his own purposes, unconnected with his work (a 'frolic of his own').

Facts: Manoj drives a delivery van for SpeedCart. On a Sunday, when he is off duty, he takes the van from the depot without permission to drive his family to a wedding in another town, and negligently injures a cyclist, Farah.

Is SpeedCart liable to Farah?
options: No, because Manoj was using the van for his own purposes, unconnected with his work.
Yes, because Manoj is a SpeedCart employee and was driving its van.
Yes, because taking the van was an authorised act done in an unauthorised manner.
No, because Farah should have avoided the van.
questions.explanation: Manoj was off duty and drove without permission for a family trip—a frolic of his own, not the company's work. Ownership of the van and his status as an employee are not enough; there was no authorised act to perform.

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: A person who voluntarily consents to a known risk cannot claim damages for harm resulting from it (volenti non fit injuria). However, a person who takes a risk to rescue others from a danger created by the defendant's negligence is not treated as having consented to that risk.

Facts: Gopal negligently leaves his bullock cart unattended on a busy market street. The bullocks bolt towards a group of schoolchildren. Ravi, a shopkeeper, runs out and stops the animals, saving the children but suffering serious injuries.

Can Ravi recover damages from Gopal?
options: Yes, because a rescuer of people endangered by the defendant's negligence is not treated as consenting to the risk.
No, because Ravi knowingly and voluntarily exposed himself to the risk.
No, because Gopal did not intend the bullocks to bolt.
Yes, but only if one of the children was actually injured.
questions.explanation: The general volenti rule would bar a person who knowingly takes a risk, but the principle's exception covers rescuers facing a danger created by the defendant's negligence. Intention is irrelevant to negligence, and the children need not be harmed for the rescuer to recover.

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: Communication of an acceptance is complete as against the proposer when it is put in the course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the acceptor's power. A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer.
